concept.name: Intracommodity spread
concept.definition: A spread involving two different delivery months of the same commodity — the CFTC glossary defines the interdelivery spread as exactly this and notes it is also called an intracommodity spread. It is functionally identical to the futures calendar spread: the trader is long one month and short another of the same contract.
concept.intuition: Same commodity, different months: you trade the shape of one market's own curve rather than its level.
concept.mechanics: Buy one delivery month and simultaneously sell another delivery month of the same futures contract. The position isolates the calendar-spread component of the term structure — carrying charges, storage economics, and seasonal supply — and is quoted and margined as a spread, often at reduced margin versus outrights.
concept.formula: Spread price = F(T1) - F(T2) for delivery months T1 != T2 of the same contract.
concept.failure_modes: The two months can decouple sharply around delivery events — first notice day, position-limit liquidations, or deliverable-supply squeezes can move the near leg violently while the deferred leg barely reacts. Low liquidity in back months raises execution risk on the spread.
concept.misconceptions: Because both legs are the same commodity, traders assume the position is nearly riskless; in reality old-crop/new-crop and front-month squeezes produce some of the largest moves in futures markets. 'Intracommodity' and 'calendar' spreads are the same structure, not distinct strategies.
concept.example: Buying July wheat and selling December wheat is an intracommodity spread: the position profits if July gains relative to December, e.g. when old-crop supplies tighten into summer.

citations.source: CFTC Futures Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
